note: Programmatic SEO matrix for quickwell.app, rendered to /strategies/<slug>/ by scripts/seo/build.mjs. Schema per CEO (strategy archetype x asset_context). Every computed figure comes from the tested engine in utility-pipeline/js/engine.mjs at build time. HARD RULES: no live/fabricated ticker data (examples are clearly-labeled illustrations, not current prices or recommendations); educational copy only (no 'safe'/'guaranteed' claims). Multi-expiration strategies (poor-man's covered call, calendar, diagonal) are 'structural' — no fabricated payoff, since pricing the back-month leg needs a volatility model.

rows.name: Covered Calls on High-Dividend Blue Chips
rows.outlook: You own the shares, are neutral-to-mildly-bullish, and want income on top of the dividend.
rows.legs: Hold 100 shares and sell one call against them. The premium is income now; if the stock is called away you sell at the strike.
rows.summary: A covered call turns shares you already hold into an income position: you collect a premium, cap your upside at the strike, and keep any dividend paid before assignment.
rows.when: Income-focused holders often pair covered calls with high-dividend blue chips: the dividend and the premium stack, and such names tend to grind rather than gap, so a capped upside stings less. The real trade-off is early assignment — when a call's remaining time value drops below the next dividend, the holder may exercise early to capture it, so watch the ex-dividend date.
rows.risk: The premium only cushions the first part of a decline; you keep the stock's full downside below breakeven, and your upside is capped at the strike. A deep in-the-money call can be assigned the day before the stock goes ex-dividend.

rows.name: Covered Calls on High-Volatility Tech
rows.outlook: You own a volatile growth name and want to harvest its rich option premium.
rows.legs: Hold 100 shares and sell an out-of-the-money call. Higher implied volatility means a fatter premium — and a bigger cushion — than a calm stock pays.
rows.summary: Writing covered calls on high-volatility stocks collects an outsized premium thanks to elevated implied volatility, building a larger downside buffer while capping the upside at the strike.
rows.when: Traders choose a further out-of-the-money strike here so a breakout isn't capped too early, while still collecting a large premium. The catch is the one that matters most on growth names: if the stock gaps far past your strike, you forgo the move above it.
rows.risk: Volatile stocks can fall hard and fast; the premium cushions only the first part of a drop. And the whole point of owning a growth name — the giant upside — is exactly what the sold call gives away above the strike.

rows.name: Covered Calls Before Earnings
rows.outlook: You hold the shares into an earnings date and want to sell premium while it's inflated.
rows.legs: Sell a short-dated call just before earnings, when its premium is puffed up by high implied volatility, then let that volatility collapse after the report.
rows.summary: Selling a covered call right before earnings captures option pricing at its most inflated. Implied volatility climbs into the event and drops sharply the morning after — the 'IV crush' — which can profit the short call even if the stock moves.
rows.when: The appeal is the IV crush: a large part of the call's value can evaporate overnight once the uncertainty is resolved. The danger is a big beat or miss — a sharp gap up caps your shares at the strike, and a gap down is only lightly cushioned by the premium.
rows.risk: Earnings are binary. A gap through your strike caps the upside; a gap down leaves you long the stock with only the premium as a buffer. The IV crush helps the option, not the shares.

rows.name: Cash-Secured Puts in Market Corrections
rows.outlook: You'd be glad to own a quality name lower, and you set aside the cash to buy it.
rows.legs: Sell a put at a strike you'd buy at and hold the cash to cover assignment. If assigned you buy at the strike; if not, you keep the premium.
rows.summary: A cash-secured put pays you to wait for a price you'd buy at. During a correction, fear inflates premiums, so you're paid more for standing ready — and your effective entry, if assigned, is the strike minus the premium.
rows.when: Pullbacks raise implied volatility across the board, so the income for underwriting a stock you want is larger. The discipline is in sizing and strike choice: a correction can deepen, and a short put goes in-the-money fast as the market falls.
rows.risk: Your downside is close to owning the stock: if it keeps falling you're assigned at the strike and ride it down, cushioned only by the premium. 'Cash-secured' means the cash is reserved, not that the trade is low-risk.

rows.name: Cash-Secured Puts on Range-Bound Indexes
rows.outlook: You want steady premium income on the broad market without single-stock surprises.
rows.legs: Sell puts on a broad index product and hold the collateral. Broad indexes diversify away single-company headline risk.
rows.summary: Selling cash-secured puts on broad indexes collects time-decay income on the whole market, with none of the overnight gap risk of a single earnings report or lawsuit.
rows.when: Because an index rarely gaps the way one stock can, the focus shifts to turning the collateral over efficiently and choosing strikes with room below the range. It's an income approach for a market you expect to chop sideways, not rocket.
rows.risk: An index can still fall in a broad sell-off, and a short put goes in-the-money with it. The diversification removes company-specific shocks, not market risk; your collateral is committed the whole time.

rows.name: Bull Put Spreads on Momentum Stocks
rows.outlook: You expect an uptrending stock to stay above a support level.
rows.legs: Sell an out-of-the-money put and buy a further out-of-the-money put, opening for a net credit beneath the trend.
rows.summary: A bull put spread is a defined-risk credit trade placed below a rising stock: you keep the credit if it holds above your short strike, and the long put caps the loss if the trend breaks.
rows.when: Traders set the short strike beneath a support band (say a rising moving average) to sell premium into momentum with a known worst case. A common plan is to take profits around half the max gain rather than hold to expiration.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the width minus the credit, well above the credit collected, and it happens if the stock drops below the lower strike. A momentum break or a flash crash is the risk.

rows.name: Bear Call Spreads on Overvalued Stocks
rows.outlook: You expect an overextended stock to stall or fall, staying below a resistance level.
rows.legs: Sell an out-of-the-money call and buy a higher call, opening for a net credit above the price.
rows.summary: A bear call spread sells premium above an overextended stock with a capped loss: you profit if it stays below your short strike, and the long call caps the damage on a squeeze.
rows.when: The short strike goes above a resistance ceiling on a high-beta name. The defining risk is a short squeeze — these stocks can rip higher violently — so the long call that caps the loss is the whole point.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the width minus the credit, realized above the higher strike. Overvalued does not mean it can't go higher first; a squeeze is exactly what breaches this spread.

rows.name: Iron Condors in Low-VIX Markets
rows.outlook: You expect the market to stay range-bound while volatility is compressed.
rows.legs: Sell a put spread below and a call spread above, both for credit, defining a range you want price to stay inside.
rows.summary: An iron condor is a defined-risk, range-bound credit trade. In a low-VIX regime premiums are thin, so the challenge is collecting enough while keeping the short strikes far enough out to survive a volatility snap-back.
rows.when: When the fear index is low, credits shrink, so condors are placed with wider, further-out strikes and a smaller credit accepted on purpose — to avoid an immediate breach if volatility reverts to its mean and the market starts moving again.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is larger than the credit and occurs past either short strike. A condor is short volatility: a sharp move either way, or a volatility spike, works against it, and there are two sides to defend.

rows.name: Iron Condors Before Earnings
rows.outlook: You expect a stock to stay within its implied move through earnings.
rows.legs: Sell a put spread and a call spread outside the market's expected move, collecting an inflated credit just before the report.
rows.summary: A pre-earnings iron condor sells the inflated implied volatility ahead of a report, with both wings capping the loss. It profits from the volatility crush if the stock lands inside the expected move.
rows.when: The method is to read the expected move from option prices, place the short strikes outside it, and often close the day after the report once the volatility crush has done its work — to avoid carrying ongoing trend risk.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is larger than the credit and happens if the stock gaps past a short strike. Earnings are binary; the expected move is a probability, not a fence, and a surprise can blow through a wing.

rows.name: Bull Call Spreads on Breakouts
rows.outlook: You expect a stock breaking resistance to continue toward a target.
rows.legs: Buy a call near the breakout level and sell a higher call at your target, paying a net debit that caps the upside.
rows.summary: A bull call spread backs a breakout with defined risk: cheaper than an outright call, with profit capped at the higher strike and loss limited to the debit if the breakout fails.
rows.when: The long strike sits near the breakout, the short strike near a technical target (a measured move or next resistance). Defining risk matters because breakouts fail and reverse often, trapping buyers — here the loss is fixed at the debit.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the debit paid, if the stock falls back below the lower strike. Time decay works against the position, and a failed breakout is the classic way it loses.

rows.name: Bear Put Spreads for Downturns
rows.outlook: You expect a cyclical name or sector to fall, and want a defined-risk hedge.
rows.legs: Buy a put near the money and sell a lower put, paying a net debit that caps the downside profit and cheapens the hedge.
rows.summary: A bear put spread profits from a decline with defined risk — cheaper than an outright put because the short leg offsets part of the cost — making it a common portfolio hedge into a cyclical downturn.
rows.when: Used to hedge long equity exposure or express a bearish macro view. Selling the lower put trims the premium of an expensive long put during a pullback, in exchange for capping the profit at the lower strike.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the debit paid, if the stock closes above the higher strike. The move has to happen before expiration, and a V-shaped bounce leaves the hedge expiring worthless.

rows.name: Long Straddle for Biotech Catalysts
rows.outlook: You expect a large move but not the direction — typical around a binary event.
rows.legs: Buy a call and a put at the same strike and expiration. You pay for both, so the position starts at a loss and needs a move to pay off.
rows.summary: A long straddle is a bet on a big move in either direction. You buy a call and a put at the same strike; your loss is capped at what you paid, and you profit only if the stock moves far enough past either breakeven.
rows.when: Traders use straddles ahead of binary events such as a biotech FDA decision, where the outcome can gap the stock sharply up or down. The catch is that options are priced for that uncertainty — implied volatility is high going in, so you pay up, and if the move is smaller than priced, or the decision slips, the position loses value.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the full premium paid, realized if the stock sits near the strike at expiration. High implied volatility before the event means you're paying up; a muted reaction or a delay works against you quickly.

rows.name: Long Strangle for Macro Rate Decisions
rows.outlook: You expect a large move but not the direction, and want a cheaper entry than a straddle.
rows.legs: Buy an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put. Both cost less than at-the-money options, so the entry is cheaper — but the underlying has to travel further to pay off.
rows.summary: A long strangle is a lower-cost cousin of the straddle: you buy an OTM call and an OTM put, pay less, and need a bigger move to profit. Loss is capped at the premium paid.
rows.when: Used around macro events — an FOMC rate decision or a major data release — that can reprice a whole index. The lower entry cost is the appeal; the trade-off is wider breakevens, so a moderate move can still lose.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the premium paid, in the zone between the two strikes. Because both options start out-of-the-money, a move that isn't big enough leaves both worthless.

rows.name: Protective Collar for Unrealized Gains
rows.outlook: You hold a stock that has risen, want to protect the gain, and will accept a capped upside to pay for it.
rows.legs: Own the shares, buy a protective put below the price for a floor, and sell a call above the price whose premium pays for the put — often a 'zero-cost collar.'
rows.summary: A protective collar brackets a stock you own: a bought put sets a floor you can't fall below, and a sold call caps your upside and pays for the put. It locks a range around an unrealized gain without selling the shares.
rows.when: Long-term holders use collars to defend a large unrealized gain through an uncertain stretch without triggering a taxable sale. The cost is your upside — if the stock keeps running, you're capped at the call strike.
rows.risk: Below the put strike you're protected, but the cap means you forgo gains above the call strike, and a sold call can be assigned early, costing an upcoming dividend. 'Zero-cost' refers to the option premiums netting out, not to giving up nothing — you're trading away upside.

rows.name: Poor Man's Covered Call with LEAPS
rows.outlook: You're bullish long-term but want stock-like exposure for a fraction of the cost.
rows.legs: Buy a deep in-the-money, long-dated call (a LEAPS) to stand in for 100 shares, then sell near-term out-of-the-money calls against it, month after month.
rows.summary: A poor man's covered call replaces the stock in a covered call with a long-dated deep-ITM call, cutting the capital outlay sharply while still letting you sell calls for income.
rows.when: Traders pick a long call with a high delta (around 0.80+) so it tracks the stock closely, and structure the short call so its premium more than covers the long call's time decay. The appeal is capital efficiency; the cost is that the LEAPS has no dividend and does decay.
rows.risk: This is a two-expiration, diagonal position, so the profit at the short call's expiration depends on the LEAPS's remaining value — which is set by implied volatility and time, not a fixed formula. Your capital at risk is the LEAPS premium; a sharp drop can hurt a leveraged position more than owning shares outright.

rows.name: Leveraged Covered Calls on Dividend Stocks
rows.outlook: You want covered-call income on a dividend name without paying full share price — and you accept giving up the dividend.
rows.legs: Run a poor man's covered call on a dividend stock: a long-dated deep-ITM call stands in for the shares, and you sell near-term calls against it.
rows.summary: A LEAPS-backed covered call amplifies income on a dividend grower for less capital — but because an option holder collects no dividend, the premium you harvest has to outweigh the dividend you give up.
rows.when: The key comparison is explicit: the call premiums you collect versus the cash dividend you'd have received owning the shares. It can be more capital-efficient, but only if the premium income clears the forgone dividend plus the LEAPS's time decay.
rows.risk: Same two-expiration caveat as any poor man's covered call — the payoff at the short expiry depends on the LEAPS's remaining value, set by volatility and time. And you give up the dividend, which is often the whole reason to hold the stock.

rows.name: Calendar Spreads in VIX Backwardation
rows.outlook: You expect near-term volatility, now higher than longer-term, to settle back down.
rows.legs: Sell a short-dated option and buy a longer-dated option at the same strike. The near leg decays faster than the far leg, which is where the profit comes from.
rows.summary: A calendar spread profits from the different speeds at which near- and far-dated options lose value. In VIX backwardation — when short-term volatility spikes above long-term — the front leg is richly priced to sell.
rows.when: The thesis is mean reversion: during panic the term structure inverts (backwardation), and a calendar sells the inflated front month against a cheaper back month, profiting as volatility normalizes and the front leg decays.
rows.risk: This is a two-expiration position: its value at the front expiration depends on the back-month option's price then, which is driven by implied volatility — so there's no fixed max-profit number. Your capital at risk is the net debit paid; a continued volatility spike or a large directional move can work against it.

rows.name: Diagonal Spreads for Recovery
rows.outlook: You expect a slow, grinding recovery higher rather than a sharp spike.
rows.legs: Buy a longer-dated call at a lower strike and sell a shorter-dated call at a higher strike — part directional bet, part income from the decaying front call.
rows.summary: A diagonal spread blends a calendar and a vertical: a long back-month call gives bullish exposure while repeatedly sold front-month calls bring in income as a stock drifts higher.
rows.when: Suited to a slow bullish turn. The plan is to let each front-month call decay toward worthless, then sell another ('rolling up' the strike as price rises), while the long back-month leg gains value as the stock recovers.
rows.risk: A two-expiration position again: the payoff when the front call expires depends on the back-month call's remaining value, set by volatility and time, so no single max-profit figure applies. Capital at risk is the net debit; a fast spike can see the short call run past you before you roll.

educational.name: The Options Wheel on Core Holdings
educational.outlook: A repeatable income loop on a high-conviction stock you're happy to own for the long run.
educational.summary: The Wheel is a loop, not a single trade. You sell cash-secured puts on a core holding you'd happily own; if assigned, you sell covered calls against the shares; if they're called away, you start again.
steps: Sell a cash-secured put at a strike you'd buy at. Collect the premium.
If it expires worthless, repeat. If assigned, you own the shares at an effective price of strike minus premium.
Sell a covered call against the shares. Collect that premium too.
If the call expires worthless, sell another. If the shares are called away, return to step one.
educational.when: Run on long-term core holdings you genuinely want to own, because every step assumes you may end up holding the stock. Over multiple cycles the stacked premiums lower your effective cost basis — the number worth tracking across assignments.
educational.risk: You carry full ownership risk whenever you hold the shares; a serious decline is the Wheel's real danger, and no amount of premium fully offsets it. Assignments also create tax lots worth tracking. Only run it on stock you'd hold through a drawdown.

educational.name: The Options Wheel on Liquid ETFs
educational.outlook: The same income loop, run on an ultra-liquid, broadly diversified fund.
educational.summary: Running the Wheel on a highly liquid ETF trades the bigger premiums of single stocks for smoother behavior, tight bid-ask spreads and diversified exposure — easier to scale and roll.
educational.when: Liquid ETFs fill at pennies-wide spreads, so you lose less to friction entering, rolling and scaling across many contracts. The smoother volatility profile means fewer gap shocks than single names, at the cost of smaller premiums.
educational.risk: A broad fund still falls in a market sell-off, and you're assigned into it — diversification removes company risk, not market risk. Premiums are thinner than on single stocks, so returns lean on consistency and turnover, not big individual credits.
